iut_type: Profile (A2DP/AVRCP) version mismatch between current and prior registration -- ICS-inheritance exemption strategy versus minimal-scope PTS testing when versions differ
customer_question: We were told that Including the prior FY23 QDID lets us inherit its profile ICS and avoid separate profile testing -- but this time our host references a component with newer profile versions (A2DP 1.4, AVRCP 1.6.2) than the prior registration used (A2DP 1.3.2, AVRCP 1.5). Does the test-avoidance method still work despite this version difference?
question_variants: If the new profile ICS doesn't add any new supported features beyond what the old registration covered, can we still avoid testing?
If we do need to update the ICS to the newer profile versions, can we limit how much new testing is required?
actual_issue: The customer's new registration referenced a host component with newer A2DP and AVRCP profile versions than what was declared in the prior (FY23) registration being carried forward, raising the question of whether the previously-recommended profile-test-avoidance strategy (inheriting ICS from the prior QDID) still applied, and if not, how much new testing would actually be required.
plain_english_explanation: Including the prior FY23 QDID and inheriting its profile ICS at the ICS level avoids separate profile testing and report uploads -- but this method only works if the new registration's actual profile ICS doesn't add any new supported items beyond what the FY23 ICS already covered. If FY26's profile functionality is identical to FY23's, the inheritance method is recommended without reservation. In this case, however, the host component's higher profile versions (A2DP 1.4 vs. 1.3.2, AVRCP 1.6.2 vs. 1.5) meant the ICS would need to be updated to reflect the newer versions, and any such ICS update automatically triggers new A2DP and AVRCP test requirements in the registration system -- the version mismatch could not simply be inherited away. However, the resulting new test scope can still be minimized: running PTS testing specifically for A2DP and AVRCP (not a broader retest of other profiles or layers) and uploading the resulting test report allows the ICS update to proceed while keeping the actual testing burden limited to just those two profiles.
consultant_answer: The ICS-inheritance method only avoids testing if your new registration's profile ICS doesn't add any new supported items beyond what the FY23 ICS already covered. Since your host's A2DP and AVRCP versions are newer than what FY23 declared, updating the ICS to reflect them will trigger new test requirements for those two profiles specifically -- this can't be avoided via inheritance. The good news is the resulting test scope can be kept minimal: run PTS testing for just A2DP and AVRCP and upload that report, which lets the ICS update proceed without triggering a broader retest.
decision_logic: When considering whether a prior registration's profile ICS can be inherited to avoid new profile testing, check whether the new registration's actual referenced component supports any profile version or feature beyond what the prior ICS already declared -- if it's identical, inheritance avoids testing entirely; if newer profile versions are involved, the ICS must be updated (triggering new test requirements for just those specific profiles), but running targeted PTS testing for only the affected profiles keeps the resulting scope minimal rather than triggering a broader retest.
final_recommendation: Before assuming a profile-test-avoidance strategy will fully apply to a new registration, explicitly verify whether the newly-referenced component's profile versions match the prior registration's declared ICS -- if newer versions are involved, proactively recommend targeted PTS testing for just the affected profiles to keep the resulting test scope minimal rather than letting the customer discover the broader requirement only after attempting the ICS edit.
risk_if_done_wrong: Assuming the ICS-inheritance method fully avoids testing without checking for profile version differences could result in an unexpected test requirement discovered late in the process, while failing to recommend the targeted minimal-scope PTS approach could result in a customer unnecessarily commissioning a broader, more expensive retest.
